'''''Bambusa vulgaris''''',  '''common bamboo''', is an open-clump type [[bamboo]] species. It is native to [[Bangladesh]], [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]], [[Southeast Asia]], and to the province of [[Yunnan]] in southern [[China]], but it has been widely cultivated in many other places and has become naturalized in several regions.<ref>[https://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=399113 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref name=Dieter>Dieter Ohrnberger, ''The bamboos of the world'', pages 279–280, Elsevier, 1999, {{ISBN|978-0-444-50020-5}}</ref> Among bamboo species, it is one of the largest and most easily recognized.<ref name=Pamphlets>''Biology Pamphlets'' (Volume 741), page 15, [[University of California]], 1895</ref><ref name=Louppe>D. Louppe, A.A. Oteng-Amoako and M. Brink, ''Timbers'' (vol. 1), pages 100–103, [[Plant Resources of Tropical Africa|PROTA]], 2008, {{ISBN|978-90-5782-209-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Bambusa vulgaris {{!}} Bamboo Info |url=https://www.bambooinfo.in/species/db/bambusa-vulgaris.asp |website=www.bambooinfo.in}}</ref>

==Description==
[[Image:Golden Bambo stem.jpg|thumb|Close-up of the golden bamboo stem]]
''Bambusa vulgaris'' forms moderately loose clumps and has no thorns.<ref name=Magnolio>Flora of North America Editorial Committee, ''Magnoliophyta: Commelinidae'', page 22, Oxford University Press, 2007, {{ISBN|978-0-19-531071-9}}</ref> It has lemon-yellow [[culm (botany)|culms]] (stems) with green stripes and dark green leaves.<ref name=Oz>[http://www.bamboo-oz.com.au/species/B_vulgarisVittata.html ''Bambusa vulgaris''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829110328/http://bamboo-oz.com.au/species/B_vulgarisVittata.html |date=2007-08-29 }}, OzBamboo; Retrieved: 2007-12-19</ref> Stems are not straight, not easy to split, inflexible, thick-walled, and initially strong.<ref name=Prota>[http://database.prota.org/dbtw-wpd/exec/dbtwpub.dll?ac=qbe_query&bu=http://database.prota.org/search.htm&tn=protab~1&qb0=and&qf0=Species+Code&qi0=Bambusa+vulgaris&rf=Webdisplay Babusa vulgaris] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181002152746/http://database.prota.org/dbtw-wpd/exec/dbtwpub.dll?ac=qbe_query&bu=http%3A%2F%2Fdatabase.prota.org%2Fsearch.htm&tn=protab~1&qb0=and&qf0=Species+Code&qi0=Bambusa+vulgaris&rf=Webdisplay |date=2018-10-02 }}, Protabase, Plant Resources of Tropical Africa</ref> The densely tufted culms grow {{convert|10|-|20|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|4|-|10|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} thick.<ref name=Dieter/><ref name=Rao>A. N. Rao, V. Ramanatha Rao and [[John Dransfield]], ''Priority species of bamboo and rattan'', page 25, Bioversity International, 1998, {{ISBN|978-92-9043-491-7}}</ref> 
Culms are basally straight or flexuose (bent alternately in different directions), drooping at the tips. Culm walls are slightly thick.<ref name=eFloras>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242307754 Bambusa vulgaris], Flora of China, eFloras.com</ref>
Nodes are slightly inflated. [[Plant stem|Internodes]] are {{convert|20|-|45|cm|in|abbr=on}}. Several branches develop from mid-culm nodes and above. Culm leaves are [[deciduous]] with dense [[Leaf#Surface|pubescence]].<ref name=Magnolio/> Leaf blades are narrowly [[lanceolate]].<ref name=eFloras/>

Flowering is not common, and there are no seeds. Fruits are rare due to low pollen viability caused by irregular [[meiosis]].<ref name=Louppe/> At the interval of several decades, the whole population of an area blooms at once,<ref name=Whistler>[[W. Arthur Whistler]], ''Tropical ornamentals: a guide'', pages 77–78, Timber Press, 2000, {{ISBN|978-0-88192-475-6}}</ref> and individual stems bear a large number of flowers.<ref name=Louppe/> Vegetation propagates through clump division, by [[rhizome]], stem and branch cutting, [[layering (horticulture)|layering]], and [[marcotting]].<ref name=Rao/><ref name=Louppe2>D. Louppe, A.A. Oteng-Amoako and M. Brink (edit.), ''Timbers 1'' (Volume 7), PROTA, 2008, {{ISBN|978-90-5782-209-4}}</ref> The easiest and most practised cultivation method is culm or branch cutting. In the Philippines, the best results were obtained from one-node cuttings from the lower parts of six-month-old culms.<ref name=Louppe/> When a stem dies, the clump usually survives.<ref name=Louppe/> A clump can grow out of stem used for poles, fences, props, stakes, or posts.<ref name=Louppe2/> Its rhizomes extend up to 80 cm before turning upward to create open, fast-spreading clumps.<ref name=Meredith/> The easy propagation of ''B. vulgaris'' explains its seemingly wild occurrence.<ref name=Louppe/>

The average chemical composition is [[cellulose]] 41–44%, [[pentosan]]s 21–23%, [[lignin]] 26–28%, [[Ash (analytical chemistry)|ash]] 1.7–1.9%, and [[silica]] 0.6–0.7%.<ref name=Prota/>

==Taxonomy==
The bambusoid taxa have long been considered the most "primitive" grasses, mostly because of the presence of [[bracts]], indeterminate [[inflorescence]]s, pseudospikelets (units of [[inflorescence]] or flower clusters and [[glume]]s or leaf-like structures in woody bamboos that is similar to [[spikelet]]s or clumps of grass<ref>Londofo & Clark, "[http://www.botanicus.org/primeocr/mbgserv14/botanicus5/b13058551/31753003431209/31753003431209_0064.txt New Taxa of Guadua] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304060204/http://www.botanicus.org/primeocr/mbgserv14/botanicus5/b13058551/31753003431209/31753003431209_0064.txt |date=2016-03-04 }}", botanicus.org</ref><ref>"[http://www.biology-online.org/dictionary/Spikelets Spikelets]", Biology Online</ref>), and [[flower]]s with three [[lodicule]]s (tiny scale-like structure at the bottom of a [[floret]]s or clump of grass flowers, found between [[lemma (botany)|lemma]], the lowest part of spikelets, and sexual organs of the flower), six [[stamen]]s, and three [[stigma (botany)|stigmas]].<ref name="Clark, LG 1995">Clark, LG, W Zhang, JF Wendel. 1995. A Phylogeny of the Grass Family (Poaceae) Based on ndhF Sequence Data. Systematic Botany 20(4): 436–460.</ref> Bamboos are some of the fastest growing plants in the world.<ref name="Farrelly">{{cite book |last=Farrelly |first=David |title=The Book of Bamboo |publisher=Sierra Club Books |year=1984 |isbn=978-0-87156-825-0 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/bookofbamboo00farr }}</ref>

''B. vulgaris'' is a species of the large genus ''[[Bambusa]]'' of the  clumping bamboo tribe [[Bambuseae]],<ref name=Kew-2>{{cite web|title=Bambusa|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/browse/A/Poaceae/Bambusa/|work=The Plant List, RBG Kew|access-date=24 January 2012}}</ref> which are found largely in [[Tropics|tropical]] and [[subtropical]] areas of Asia, especially in the wet tropics.<ref name="Farrelly"/> The pachymorph ([[sympodial]] or superposed in such a way as to imitate a simple axis) [[rhizome]] system of clumping bamboos expands horizontally by only a short distance each year.<ref name=Complete>"[http://www.completebamboo.com/bamboo_runners_clumpers.html Bamboo Biology – Runners vs. Clumpers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130720083932/http://www.completebamboo.com/bamboo_runners_clumpers.html |date=2013-07-20 }}", Complete Bamboo, Bamboo Plant Information Resource</ref> The shoots emerge in a tight or open habit (group), depending on the species; common bamboo has open groups. Regardless of the degree of openness of each species' clumping habit, none of the clumpers are considered invasive.<ref>"[https://tropicalbamboo.com/Bamboo_clumping.asp Clumping Vs Running Bamboos]", Tropical Bamboo</ref> New culms can only form at the very tip of the rhizome.<ref name=Complete/> The Bambuseae are a group of [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[evergreen]]s in subfamily [[Bambusoideae]], characterized by having three stigmata and tree-like behavior.<ref>Judd, WS, CS Campbell, EA Kellogg, PF Stevens, MJ Donoghue [eds.]. 2008. Plant Systematics: A Phylogenetic Approach, 296–301. Sinauer Associates, Inc., Sunderland, Massachusetts USA.</ref>

===Cultivars===
At least three groupings of ''B. vulgaris'' [[cultivar]]s can be distinguished:<ref name=Prota/>

* Plants with green stems
* Golden bamboo (plants with yellow stems): Plants always contain yellow stems, often with green stripes of different intensity. Usually the stems have thicker walls than those of the green stem group. This group is often distinguished as ''Bambusa vulgaris'' var. ''striata''.
* Buddha's belly bamboo: Plants with stems up to about {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, {{convert|1|-|3|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter, green, with {{convert|4|-|10|cm|in|adj=on|sigfig=1|abbr=on}}-long inflated internodes in the lower part. This group is often distinguished as ''B. v.'' var. ''wamin''.

The more common cultivars are:<ref name=Hatch>Laurence Hatch, ''[[Cultivar]]s of Woody Plants'' (Volume I: A-G), section Bambusa, TCR Press, 2007, {{ISBN|978-0-9714465-0-2}}</ref>

* 'Aureovariegata' (''B. v.'' var.'' aureovariegata'' <small>Beadle</small><ref name=Kew/>): With rich golden yellow culms striped in green, sometimes in very thin lines,<ref name=Hatch/> it is the most common variety of ''B. vulgaris''.<ref name=Clay/>
* 'Striata' (''Bambusa vulgaris var. striata'' <small>(Lodd. ex Lindl.) Gamble</small><ref name=Kew/>): A common variety, smaller in size than other varieties, with bright yellow [[internode (botany)|internode]]s and random markings with longitudinal stripes in light and deep green.<ref name=Dieter/>
* 'Wamin' (''B. v.'' f. ''waminii'' <small>T.H.Wen</small><ref name=Kew/>): It is smaller in size than other varieties with short and flattened internodes. Likely to have originated in South China, 'Wamin' bamboo is spread throughout East Asia, Southeast Asia, and South Asia.<ref name=Dieter/> Basally inflated internodes give it a unique appearance.<ref name=Bio>''Bamboo The Amazing Grass'', page 44, Bioversity International</ref>
* 'Vittata' (''B. v.'' f. ''vittata'' <small>(Rivière & C.Rivière) McClure</small><ref name=Kew/>): A common variety that grows up to {{convert|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, it has [[barcode]]-like striping in green.<ref name=Hatch/>
* 'Kimmei': Culms yellow, striped with green<ref name=Hatch/>
* 'Maculata': Green culms mottled with black, turning mostly black with aging<ref name=Hatch/>
* 'Wamin Striata': Grows up to {{convert|5|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, light green striped in dark green, with swollen lower internodes<ref name=Hatch/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[Image:Bamboos_bambusa_vulgaris_sao_paulo_botanical_garden_brazil.jpg|thumb|left|''B. vulgaris'' at the [[São Paulo]]'s Botanical Garden, [[São Paulo (state)|SP]], Brazil]]

Common bamboo is the most widely grown bamboo throughout the tropics and subtropics. Although mostly known only from cultivation, spontaneous (non[[domesticated]]), escaped, and [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] populations exist throughout the tropics and subtropics in and outside Asia.<ref name=Dieter/><ref name=Louppe/> ''B. vulgaris'' is widely cultivated in [[East Asia|East]], [[Southeast Asia|Southeast]], and [[South Asia]], as well as tropical Africa including Madagascar.<ref name=Dieter/><ref name=Louppe/> It is highly concentrated in the [[Indomalayan realm|Indomalayan]] [[rainforest]]s.<ref name=Oz/> The species is one of the most successful bamboos in [[Pakistan]], [[Tanzania]], and [[Brazil]].<ref name=Lobovikov>Maxim Lobovikov, Lynn Ball and María Guardia, ''World bamboo resources'', pages 13–18, [[Food and Agriculture Organization]], 2007, {{ISBN|978-92-5-105781-0}}</ref>

Popular as a hothouse plant by the 1700s, it was one of the earliest bamboo species introduced into Europe.<ref name=Meredith/> It is believed to have been introduced to Hawaii in the time of Captain [[James Cook]] (the late 18th century), and is the most popular ornamental plant there.<ref name=Clay>Horace Freestone Clay, James C. Hubbard and Rick Golt, ''Tropical Exotics'', page 10, University of Hawaii Press, 1987, {{ISBN|978-0-8248-1127-3}}</ref> ''B. vulgaris'' is widely cultivated in the [[United States|USA]] and [[Puerto Rico]], apparently since introduction by Spaniards in 1840.<ref name=Dieter/> It may have been the first foreign species introduced into the United States by Europeans.<ref name=Meredith>Ted Jordan Meredith, ''Timber Press pocket guide to bamboos'', page 49, Timber Press, 2009, {{ISBN|978-0-88192-936-2}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:金絲竹Bambusa vulgaris 20210428210317 03.jpg|thumb|x290px]]
[[Image:Bambusa vulgaris at veluppadam.JPG|thumb|The specimen at Kerala Forest Research Institute (KFRI), Veluppadam, [[Kerala]]]]
[[File:Bambusa vulgaris Schrad. ex J.C.Wendl.jpg|thumb|''Bambusa vulgaris'' Schrad. ex J.C.Wendl. ([[Hawaii]], [[Garden of Eden Arboretum & Botanical Garden]])]]

''B. vulgaris'' grows mostly on river banks, road sides, wastelands, and open ground, generally in the low altitudes. It is a preferred species for [[erosion control]].<ref name=Oz/> It grows best under humid conditions, but can tolerate unfavorable conditions like low temperatures and drought.<ref name=Dieter/><ref name=Rao/> Though adoptable to a wide range of soils,<ref name=Dieter/>  common bamboo grows more vigorously on moist soils.<ref name=Rao/> It can tolerate frost down to {{convert|-3|°C|°F}}, and can grow on ground up to {{convert|1500|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level,<ref name=Rao/> though in higher altitudes stems grow shorter and thinner.<ref name=Louppe/> In extreme droughts, it may defoliate completely.<ref name=Louppe/>

===Pests===
The two major threats to the species are small bamboo borers (''[[Dinoderus minutus]]''), which as adults bore stems in India, China, Philippines, Australia, and Japan, and bamboo weevils (''[[Cyrtotrachelus longimanus]]''), which destroy shoots during their [[larvae|larval stage]] in South China.<ref name=Hill>D. S. Hill, ''Pests of Crops in Warmer Climates and Their Control'', page 517, Springer, 2008, {{ISBN|978-1-4020-6737-2}}</ref> Other [[Pest (organism)|pests]] include leaf blight (''[[Cercospora]]''), basal culm rot (''[[Fusarium]]''), culm sheath rot (''[[Glomerella cingulata]]''), leaf rust (''[[Kweilingia divina]]''), and leaf spots (''[[Dactylaria]]'').<ref name=Louppe/> In Bangladesh, bamboo blight caused by ''[[Sarocladium oryzae]]'' is a serious disease.<ref name=Louppe/>

==Uses==
Common bamboo has a wide variety of uses, including the stems used as fuel and the leaves used as fodder,<ref name=Louppe/><ref name=Dharani/> though a large amount of ingestion of leaves is known to cause neurological disorder among horses.<ref name=Louppe/> The worldwide production and trade of ''B. vulgaris'' is considerable, though no statistics are available.<ref name=Louppe/> It also has some disadvantages. Working and [[machining]] properties of the stems are poor, as they are not straight, not easy to split, and not flexible, but they are thick-walled and initially strong.<ref name=Louppe/> Because of high carbohydrate content, stems are susceptible to attacks from fungi and insects such as [[powderpost beetle]]s. Protection from biological threats is essential for long-term use.<ref name=Louppe/>

''B. v.'' var. ''striata'' is used as ornamental solitary or as border hedge. Its shoots boiled in water are sometimes used for medicinal qualities. Cultivated around the world, it is generally found in East, Southeast, and South Asia.<ref name=Dieter/> ''B. v.'' f. ''waminii'' is cultivated in the US and Europe in addition to Asia.<ref name=Dieter/> ''B. v.'' f. ''vittata''  is the most popular variety as an ornamental plant,<ref name=Whistler/> and is considered to be very beautiful.<ref name=Meredith/> The 'Kimmei' cultivar is mostly cultivated in Japan.<ref name=Dieter/>

===Ornamental===
It is widely used as an ornamental plant.<ref name=Dharani/><ref name=Ernest>Ernest Braunton, ''The Garden Beautiful in California'', page 50, Applewood Books, 2008, {{ISBN|978-1-4290-1281-2}}</ref> It often is planted as fences and border hedges.<ref name=Dieter/><ref name=Dharani>Najma Dharani, ''Field guide to common trees & shrubs of East Africa'', page 198, Struik, 2002, {{ISBN|978-1-86872-640-0}}</ref> It is also planted as a measure for [[erosion control]].<ref name=Louppe/>

===Construction===
The stems or culms of ''B. vulgaris'' are used for fencing and construction, especially of small, temporary shelters,<ref name=Dieter/> including flooring, roof tiles, panelling, and walls made wither with culms or split stems.<ref name=Louppe/> The culm is used to make many parts of boats including masts, rudders, outriggers, and boating poles.<ref name=Dieter/> It also is used to make furniture, basketry, windbreakers, flutes, fishing rods, tool handles, stakes, weapons, bows for fishing nets, smoking pipes, irrigation pipes, distillation pipes, and more.<ref name=Dieter/><ref name=Louppe/><ref name=Rao/>

It is used as raw material for [[paper pulp]], especially in India.<ref name=Louppe/><ref name=Rao/> Paper made from ''B. vulgaris'' has exceptional [[tearing (physics)|tear strength]], comparable to paper made of [[softwood]]. It can also be used to make particle boards and [[flexible packaging]] grade paper.<ref name=Louppe/>

===Food===
Young shoots of the plant, cooked or pickled,<ref name=Rao/> are edible and eaten throughout Asia.<ref name=Clay/> Yellow shoots remain buttercup yellow after cooking.<ref name=Oz/> A [[decoction]] of the growing tips is mixed with [[Job's tears]] (''Coix lacryma-jobi'') to make a refreshing drink in [[Mauritius]].<ref name=Louppe/> The shoots are tender and whitish pink{{clarify|date=January 2012|reason=I thought they were yellow?}}, and have a fair [[canning]] quality.<ref name=Louppe/>

A {{convert|100|g|oz|adj=on}} serving of young shoots of green-stem [[cultivar]]s has 90 g of water, 2.6 g of protein, 4.1 g of fat, 0.4 g of digestible carbohydrates, 1.1 g of insoluble [[dietary fiber]], 22.8 mg <!-- NOT micrograms -->of calcium, 37 mg of phosphorus, 1.1 mg of iron, and 3.1 mg of [[Vitamin C|ascorbic acid]]. A serving of young shoots of yellow-stem cultivars has 88 g of water, 1.8 g of protein, 7.2 g of fat, 0.0 g of digestible carbohydrates, 1.2 grams of insoluble fiber, 28.6 mg of calcium, 27.5 mg of phosphorus, and 1.4 mg of iron.<ref name=Louppe/>

=== Indigenous medicine ===
Golden bamboo is considered in many traditions across Asia to have medicinal value. Many uses are found in [[herbal medicine]], though the effects are not clinically proven. In Java, water stored in golden bamboo tubes is used as a cure of various diseases. In the Congo, its leaves are used as part of a treatment against [[measles]]; in Nigeria, an infusion of [[macerated]] leaves is taken against [[sexually transmitted disease]]s and as an [[abortifacient]] – the latter has been shown to work in rabbits.<ref name=Louppe/><ref>MT Yakubu and BB Bukoye, "[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19698826 Abortifacient potentials of the aqueous extract of Bambusa vulgaris leaves in pregnant Dutch rabbits]", PubMed, National Center for Biotechnology Information, U.S. National Library of Medicine</ref>

==Cultivation==
Though not suited for small yards, as it grows in large clumps,<ref name=Whistler/> young plants of golden bamboo can be grown in large containers.<ref name=Langenberg>Arthur Van Langenberg and Ip Kung Sau, ''Urban gardening: a Hong Kong gardener's journal'', page 38, Chinese University Press, 2006, {{ISBN|978-962-996-261-6}}</ref> Golden bamboo grows well in full sunlight or partial shade.<ref name=Clay/> Protection is important, as animals often graze on young shoots.<ref name=Louppe/> In Tanzania, management of ''B. vulgaris'' cultivation entails clearing of the ground around clumps.<ref name=Louppe/>

==Toxicity==
Among all bamboos, only shoots of ''B. vulgaris'' contains taxiphyllin (a [[cyanogenic glycoside]]) that functions as an [[enzyme inhibitor]] in the human body when released,<ref>Christopher P. Holstege, Thomas Neer, Gregory B. Saathoff, M.D. and Brent Furbee, ''Criminal Poisoning: Clinical and Forensic Perspectives'', page 65, Jones & Bartlett Learning, 2010, {{ISBN|978-0-7637-4463-2}}</ref> but [[Chemical decomposition|degrades]] readily in boiling water.<ref>I Hunter and Feng’e Yang, "[http://www.inbar.int/publication/txt/INBAR_Working_Paper_No39.htm Cyanide in Bamboo Shoots] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114162042/http://www.inbar.int/publication/txt/INBAR_Working_Paper_No39.htm |date=2012-01-14 }}", [[WHO]] ''Food Additives Series'' 30, International Network for Bamboo and Rattan</ref> It is highly toxic, and the lethal dose for humans is about 50–60 mg.<ref>S.Satya, L.M. Bal, P. Singhal and S.N Naik, ''Bamboo shoot processing: food quality and safety aspect (a review)'', 2010. Bamboo shoot
processing: food quality and safety aspect (a review), Trends Food (issue 21), pages 181–189; cited by: Chanda Vongsombath, ''[uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:406136/FULLTEXT01 Botanical repellents and pesticides traditionally used against Hematophagous invertebrates in LAO DR]''</ref> A dose of 25 mg cyanogenic glycoside fed to rats (100–120 g body weight) caused clinical signs of toxicity, including [[apnoea]], [[ataxia]], and [[paresis]].<ref>G. Speijers, "[https://www.inchem.org/documents/jecfa/jecmono/v30je18.htm Cyanogenic Glycoside]", Chemical Safety Information from Intergovernmental Organizations</ref> Horses in [[Pará]], [[Brazil]], were diagnosed with clinical signs of [[somnolence]] and severe ataxia after ingesting ''B. vulgaris''.<ref>Franklin Riet-Correa, ''Poisoning by Plants, Mycotoxins and Related Toxins'', page 292, CABI, 2011, {{ISBN|978-1-84593-833-8}}</ref> Farmers in Africa sometimes prefer to buy it rather than plant it, as they believe it harms the soil.<ref name=Karen>Karen Ann Dvořák, ''Social science research for agricultural technology development'', page 175,  International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), 1993, {{ISBN|978-0-85198-806-1}}</ref>
